title: File systems
scopeHtml:
Scope: inodes, journaling, ext4 vs XFS, page cache, fsync and durability, and a slow-disk incident.

Scope: inodes, journaling, ext4 vs XFS, page cache, fsync and durability, and a slow-disk incident.

notes.title: What a file system does
notes.html:
A file system turns a dumb array of numbered disk blocks into named files and directories. The disk (HDD or SSD) only knows "read block 8,123,456" and "write block 8,123,457". The file system adds: names, folders, sizes, permissions, timestamps, free-space tracking, and crash safety.

Layers a read() goes through on Linux:

  • VFS (virtual file system): a common interface (open, read, write, stat). It lets ext4, XFS, NFS, tmpfs, overlayfs and /proc all look the same. Key VFS objects: superblock (one mounted file system), inode (one file's metadata), dentry (a cached name-to-inode link), file (an open file with an offset).
  • Page cache: RAM holding recent file data in 4 KB pages (see the page cache section).
  • Block layer and I/O scheduler: merges and orders requests (mq-deadline, none for NVMe, bfq).

Worked example. cat /var/log/app.log of 10 MB: the kernel resolves the path component by component (var, log, app.log) through dentries, finds the inode, reads 2,560 pages of 4 KB through the page cache, with read-ahead prefetching ahead of the sequential pattern (default read-ahead 128 KB). Second run: all from RAM, about 20 times faster.

$ mount | grep ' / '
/dev/nvme0n1p2 on / type ext4 (rw,relatime,errors=remount-ro)
$ df -hT /
Filesystem     Type  Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme0n1p2 ext4  466G  211G  232G  48% /

Industry examples. Most Linux servers: ext4 (default on Debian/Ubuntu) or XFS (default on RHEL, used by many databases and Kafka brokers). Copy-on-write file systems: ZFS, Btrfs. Google's GFS/Colossus and HDFS are distributed file systems built on top of local file systems like these.

Everyday analogy. A library: the disk is the shelves with numbered slots; the file system is the catalogue that says which slots hold which book.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking the file name is stored in the file. Names live in directories; the file itself is the inode.
  • Forgetting the page cache: most reads never touch the disk.

notes.title: Inodes and directories
notes.html:
An inode is a small record describing one file: owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count, and where the data blocks are. It does not contain the name or (for big files) the data. A directory is just a special file that maps names to inode numbers.

Directory /home/amit (a file of entries)         Inode 52331
  name        inode#                              mode: -rw-r--r--
  notes.txt   52331      ------------------>      uid/gid, size 18,400
  a.sh        52340                               atime/mtime/ctime
  .           52000                               link count: 1
  ..          51000                               block map (extents) -> data

Consequences you can use in interviews:

  • Hard link: two names, one inode (link count 2). Deleting one name keeps the data. ln a b.
  • Symlink: a tiny file whose content is a path; it can dangle.
  • Delete (unlink) removes a name and decrements the link count; space is freed only when count is 0 and no process still has the file open. That is why deleting a 20 GB log while the process still writes does not free space: df still shows it full, and lsof shows (deleted).
  • mv inside one file system just rewrites directory entries (atomic rename); across file systems it is copy then delete.
  • Out of inodes: ext4 creates a fixed number of inodes at mkfs time (default one per 16 KB of space). Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while df -h shows free space.
$ df -i /var
Filesystem      Inodes   IUsed   IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/sda3      6553600 6553600       0  100% /var
$ touch /var/x
touch: cannot create '/var/x': No space left on device    # misleading: it is inodes
$ lsof +L1                                 # open files with link count 0 (deleted but held)
COMMAND  PID USER FD TYPE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
java    2310 app   7w REG 21474836480 0  9921 /var/log/app.log (deleted)

How data is found. Old ext2/3 used direct, indirect, double-indirect block pointers (slow for big files). ext4 and XFS use extents: one record says "blocks 9000 to 17191 hold file offset 0 up to 32 MB", so a large file needs few records. Directories use hashed B-trees (ext4 HTree, XFS B+tree) so a directory with a million files still looks up a name in a few reads.

Industry examples. Mail servers (Maildir) and package caches create huge numbers of small files and hit the inode limit; some use mkfs.ext4 -N or -T small to create more inodes. Docker overlay2 layers rely on hard links and inode behaviour.

Everyday analogy. The inode is the library's index card for a book; the directory entry is a note saying "the book called Dune is card 52331". Two notes can point to one card.

Common interview traps.

  • "Disk full" with free space shown: check df -i, and deleted-but-open files with lsof +L1.
  • Saying rm erases data. It drops a name; blocks are freed later and data may remain on disk.

notes.title: Journaling and crash consistency
notes.html:
A crash in the middle of a multi-step update must not leave the file system corrupt. Creating a file touches several places: the inode bitmap, the inode, the data bitmap, the data block, the directory entry. If power fails after some but not all, you get leaked blocks, two files sharing a block, or a name pointing to garbage. Old file systems ran fsck after a crash and scanned the whole disk: hours for large disks.

Journaling (write-ahead log): write the intended changes to a small log area first, mark them committed, then apply them to the real locations. After a crash, replay committed transactions and ignore incomplete ones. Recovery takes seconds, independent of disk size.

ext4 modes (data= mount option):

  • data=ordered (default): only metadata is journaled; but data blocks are forced to disk before the metadata commit. After a crash, no file points to stale garbage, though file contents may be the old version.
  • data=writeback: metadata journaled, data order not guaranteed; fastest, can expose old disk contents inside new files after a crash.
  • data=journal: both data and metadata journaled; safest, roughly halves write throughput because data is written twice.

XFS journals metadata only (a log, sized 10s to 100s of MB, can be placed on a separate device). Btrfs and ZFS use copy-on-write instead: never overwrite in place; write new blocks and atomically flip a root pointer, so there is no journal to replay.

Worked example. Create a 4 KB file in ordered mode: (1) write data block, (2) write journal blocks (inode, bitmaps, directory), (3) write commit block with a flush/barrier, (4) later checkpoint the metadata home. If power dies before (3), the transaction is discarded: the file never existed. After (3), replay re-applies it. A commit happens every commit=5 seconds by default, so up to 5 seconds of updates can be lost on a crash even though the file system is consistent.

$ dmesg | grep -i ext4
EXT4-fs (sda3): recovery complete
EXT4-fs (sda3): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode. Opts: (null)
$ tune2fs -l /dev/sda3 | grep -i journal
Journal size:             128M

Decision gravity. Journal mode is a mount option, reversible with a remount; the file system choice itself (ext4 vs XFS vs ZFS) is close to a one-way door on a populated volume (needs copy-out and re-create).

Industry examples. ext4 and XFS are the Linux defaults; NTFS, APFS and HFS+ also journal or use CoW. Databases keep their own write-ahead log (Postgres WAL, MySQL redo log), which is the same idea one level up.

Everyday analogy. A builder writes "I am about to move the wall" in a logbook before starting. If the builder disappears mid-job, the next one reads the log and finishes or undoes the job cleanly.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a journal protects your data. It protects the file system's structure; your last seconds of data may still be lost unless you call fsync.
  • Saying ordered mode journals data. It journals metadata only.

notes.title: ext4 vs XFS and other choices
notes.html:
Both are mature, journaled, extent-based. The choice depends on workload.

ext4 XFS
Max file system size 1 EiB (typically tested to 100s of TiB) 8 EiB
Max file size 16 TiB (4 KB blocks) 8 EiB
Allocation Extents, delayed allocation, multi-block allocator Extents, delayed allocation, allocation groups (parallel)
Parallel writes to many files Good Very good: each allocation group has its own lock
Shrink Yes (offline) No (can only grow)
Small file / metadata heavy Good Good; very fast delete of huge trees in modern versions
Default in Debian, Ubuntu, Android RHEL/CentOS, Oracle Linux
Typical use General purpose, boot volumes Big files, databases, Kafka, many cores, large volumes

Related options: Btrfs (CoW, snapshots, checksums, compression), ZFS (CoW, checksums, snapshots, RAID built in; ARC cache uses lots of RAM), tmpfs (RAM-backed), F2FS (flash-friendly, used on phones), overlayfs (container layers).

Key tuning knobs.

# Database volume on XFS: avoid access-time writes, large log
mount -o noatime,nodiratime /dev/nvme1n1 /var/lib/postgresql
# ext4 for a Kafka log dir (many use XFS), no atime
/dev/nvme2n1 /data/kafka xfs defaults,noatime 0 0
# Check fragmentation
xfs_db -r -c frag /dev/nvme2n1
filefrag -v /data/big.dat
  • noatime/relatime: stop writing the access time on every read. relatime (default) updates atime only if older than mtime or 24 h.
  • Delayed allocation: ext4/XFS hold data in RAM and choose disk blocks at flush time, giving contiguous extents. The cost: after a crash, a file written but not fsynced can be zero-length (the famous ext4 2009 "zero-length file" controversy, since mitigated for rename-over-old-file patterns).
  • Reserved blocks: ext4 reserves 5% for root by default. On a 10 TB data disk that is 500 GB; reduce with tune2fs -m 1.

Industry examples. Red Hat standardised on XFS for its scalability; Google's data centres have used ext4 for years; Meta runs Btrfs on large parts of its fleet; many Cassandra and Kafka guides recommend XFS or ext4 with noatime; Android moved userdata to F2FS on many devices.

Everyday analogy. Two filing systems for an office: one simple and flexible for everyday use, the other designed with many parallel clerks (allocation groups) for a huge archive.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming XFS can shrink. It cannot.
  • Picking a CoW file system for a write-heavy database without noting fragmentation and write amplification.
  • Forgetting the block size and inode count are chosen at mkfs time.

notes.title: The page cache
notes.html:
The page cache keeps file contents in spare RAM so repeated reads and many writes never reach the disk. Linux uses all free memory for it; "free" memory is wasted memory. It is why free -m shows low "free" but healthy "available".

Reads: check the cache; on a miss, read from disk and also read ahead for sequential patterns. Writes: copied into cache pages marked dirty; the call returns immediately (a write-back cache). Kernel flusher threads write dirty pages later, when they are older than vm.dirty_expire_centisecs (default 3000 = 30 s) or dirty memory exceeds thresholds.

Important thresholds (defaults, confirm for your kernel):

  • vm.dirty_background_ratio = 10: above 10% of reclaimable memory dirty, background flushing starts.
  • vm.dirty_ratio = 20: above 20%, writers are throttled and forced to write synchronously. This produces latency spikes in apps that "only write to a file".
  • vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs = 500: flusher wakes every 5 s.
$ free -m
              total  used  free  shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:          32000  9100   410     120       22490      22400
$ grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback:' /proc/meminfo
Dirty:            184320 kB
Writeback:         20480 kB
$ vmtouch -v /var/lib/postgresql/data/base/16384/16397     # how much of a file is cached
# Drop caches (testing only, never routinely):
echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches

Worked example. A service writes logs at 200 MB/s for 30 s onto a disk that sustains 150 MB/s. Cache absorbs the burst: 6 GB written, 4.5 GB flushed, 1.5 GB still dirty. If the dirty limit is 3.2 GB (20% of 16 GB), the app hits it after 64 s of the excess and every write() suddenly stalls for seconds. Visible as p99 latency spikes with iostat showing the disk 100% busy. Fixes: lower dirty_background_bytes so flushing starts early and smoothly, rate-limit, or use faster disks.

Direct I/O. Opening with O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache. Databases that manage their own buffer pool (MySQL InnoDB with innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT, Oracle) use it to avoid double caching. Postgres relies on the OS cache and keeps shared_buffers modest (about 25% of RAM).

Industry examples. Kafka famously relies on the page cache rather than its own heap cache: writes append to the log, and consumers reading recent data are served from RAM. That is why Kafka brokers should have lots of RAM left to the OS and a small JVM heap (about 6 GB).

Everyday analogy. A chef's counter: ingredients fetched from the pantry (disk) stay on the counter (RAM) for reuse; dirty plates pile up and are washed in batches. If the pile gets too tall, the chef must stop cooking and wash.

Common interview traps.

  • Seeing low "free" memory and calling it a leak. Look at available.
  • Thinking write() success means the data is on disk. It means it is in the page cache.
  • Dropping caches in production as a "fix"; it only causes a read storm.

notes.title: fsync and durability
notes.html:
fsync(fd) is the call that forces a file's dirty data (and the metadata needed to find it) to stable storage before returning. Without it, "written" data may exist only in RAM and be lost on power failure or kernel crash (a process crash alone does not lose it; the kernel still has it).

Related calls:

  • fsync(fd): data plus metadata (size, extents).
  • fdatasync(fd): data and only the metadata needed to read it back; skips timestamps. Slightly cheaper.
  • O_SYNC / O_DSYNC flags: every write behaves as if followed by fsync.
  • sync_file_range, msync for mmap'd files. syncfs for a whole file system.
  • Directory fsync: after creating or renaming a file, also fsync the parent directory, or the new name may be lost.

The safe atomic-replace pattern (used by editors, config writers, databases):

# 1. write new content to a temp file in the SAME directory
# 2. fsync the temp file
# 3. rename(tmp, final)    -- atomic on POSIX
# 4. fsync the directory
import os
def atomic_write(path, data: bytes):
    tmp = path + ".tmp"
    fd = os.open(tmp, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
    try:
        os.write(fd, data)
        os.fsync(fd)                      # data on stable storage
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.rename(tmp, path)                  # atomic switch
    dfd = os.open(os.path.dirname(path) or ".", os.O_RDONLY)
    try: os.fsync(dfd)                    # make the rename durable
    finally: os.close(dfd)

What fsync costs. On a consumer SSD a flush can take 0.5 to 5 ms; on a datacenter NVMe with power-loss protection (capacitors), often 20 to 100 microseconds; on a spinning disk, 5 to 15 ms (a rotation). A database doing one fsync per commit is limited to about 1/latency commits per second per disk: 200 commits/s at 5 ms. Hence group commit: batch many transactions into one fsync (Postgres, MySQL both do). Postgres's synchronous_commit=off risks losing the last ~600 ms of commits (3 x wal_writer_delay) but never corrupts data.

$ strace -T -e trace=fsync,fdatasync -p 3300
fdatasync(12) = 0 <0.004912>
fdatasync(12) = 0 <0.005104>      # 5 ms each: your commit rate ceiling is ~200/s
$ pg_test_fsync        # Postgres benchmark of fsync methods on your disk

The fsyncgate lesson (2018). Postgres found that after a failed fsync (I/O error), Linux marked the dirty pages clean and a retry fsync reported success while the data was lost. Postgres now PANICs on fsync failure instead of retrying. Lesson: an fsync error means your data may be gone; treat it as fatal.

Disks lie. Some drives acknowledge a flush while data is still in volatile cache. Enterprise SSDs have capacitors; cheap ones may not. Barriers/flush must be enabled (default). Test power loss with tools like diskchecker.

Decision gravity. Fsync per write is the safest and slowest; batching trades a bounded loss window for 10 to 100 times more throughput. Choose from the business: payments need fsync on commit; metrics and caches do not. Reversible by config, but data lost under a weak setting is gone for good.

Industry examples. Redis appendfsync always | everysec | no (default everysec: lose up to ~1 s). Kafka does not fsync each message by default; it relies on replication for durability (flush.messages is left unset, with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2). etcd fsyncs its WAL on every write, so slow disks cause leader elections (watch the wal_fsync_duration_seconds metric).

Everyday analogy. Writing a cheque (write) versus the bank confirming the money has moved (fsync). The slip in your pocket is not the money.

Common interview traps.

  • Using fclose/flush (user-space buffer to kernel) and assuming it is durable. There are two buffers: libc and the kernel page cache.
  • Forgetting the directory fsync after rename or create.
  • Calling fsync on a hot path per request, then wondering why throughput is 200/s.

notes.title: Putting it together: a slow disk incident
notes.html:
Scenario. An API's p99 jumps from 40 ms to 2 s every few minutes. CPU is low. The service writes an audit log and a Postgres database on the same volume.

$ iostat -x 1
Device   r/s   w/s  rkB/s   wkB/s  await  aqu-sz  %util
nvme0n1  45   2900   360   185000    18.4    53.2   99.8
$ cat /proc/pressure/io
some avg10=62.40 avg60=48.10 avg300=30.00 total=88122310
$ grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback:' /proc/meminfo
Dirty:           3145728 kB
Writeback:        982000 kB
$ sudo perf trace -s -p 4012 -- sleep 5 2>&1 | grep -E 'fsync|write'
fsync    812 calls    total 3910.2 ms    max 640.3 ms

Reading it: the disk is saturated (%util 99.8, await 18 ms, queue depth 53), dirty pages are high, the pressure stall info (/proc/pressure/io) shows 62% of time some tasks stalled on I/O, and fsync takes up to 640 ms because the journal commit must wait for a flood of other dirty data (ordered mode flushes data first). The audit log writer and the database fight for one journal.

Fixes in order of cost: put WAL/log on a separate device, lower vm.dirty_background_bytes (for example 256 MB) so writeback is smooth, batch log writes, use ionice -c3 for backups, upgrade to NVMe with power-loss protection.

Everyday analogy. One lift for both luggage trolleys and urgent doctors: the doctors wait behind the luggage.

Common interview traps.

  • Looking only at CPU and app logs. Check iostat -x, /proc/pressure/io, and fsync latency.
  • Fixing with more RAM alone: bigger dirty cache means bigger stalls when it finally flushes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• The file system maps names to inodes and inodes to extents of blocks; the VFS gives one API over ext4, XFS, tmpfs, overlayfs, NFS.
  • Inodes hold metadata, directories map names to inodes; deleting needs link count 0 and no open handles; watch df -i and lsof +L1.
  • Journaling (ext4 ordered by default, XFS metadata log) keeps structure consistent; CoW systems (ZFS, Btrfs) avoid in-place overwrites.
  • ext4: general purpose, can shrink; XFS: scalable, parallel allocation groups, cannot shrink; use noatime on data volumes.
  • The page cache makes reads fast and writes asynchronous; dirty ratio thresholds cause write stalls; Kafka and Postgres lean on it.
  • write is not durable; fsync or fdatasync plus directory fsync is; use temp file, fsync, rename, fsync dir; batch commits to amortise cost; an fsync error is fatal.
  • Debug with iostat -x, /proc/meminfo, /proc/pressure/io, strace -T, pg_test_fsync.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what happens on Linux when a program calls read() on a file, from the syscall down to the disk.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you know the layers (VFS, page cache, block layer) and why most reads never touch the disk.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: read() enters the VFS, which resolves the path through cached dentries to an inode and calls the concrete file system (ext4, XFS). The file system looks up the data in the page cache; on a hit it copies from RAM. On a miss it maps the file offset to disk blocks through extents, the block layer queues the I/O, and read-ahead prefetches following pages. The disk only ever sees "read block N".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App read() -> VFS -> ext4/XFS -> Page cache -> Block layer (scheduler) -> SSD/HDD

VFS objects: superblock (a mounted file system), inode (file metadata), dentry (cached name to inode), file (open instance with an offset). Page cache holds 4 KB pages; default read-ahead is 128 KB. Example: cat of a 10 MB log reads 2,560 pages; the second run is served from RAM about 20x faster. The block layer scheduler (mq-deadline, none for NVMe, bfq) merges and orders requests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
mount | grep ' / '
# /dev/nvme0n1p2 on / type ext4 (rw,relatime,errors=remount-ro)
df -hT /

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the file name is stored in the file; it lives in the directory.
  • Forgetting the page cache: most reads never hit the disk.
  • Believing read returns data straight from the device.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a dentry? -> A cached mapping from name to inode that speeds path lookup.
  2. What does read-ahead do? -> Prefetches sequential pages so the next read hits RAM.
  3. How would you bypass the cache? -> O_DIRECT; databases with their own buffer pool use it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior names VFS, dentry/inode/page-cache roles and ties it to why a cold cache is slow and a warm cache is fast.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a reboot or cache drop, a service's first requests were 20x slower until the page cache warmed.

questions.promptHtml: What is an inode, what is a directory, and what actually happens when you rm a file?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most "disk full but not really" incidents come from not knowing inodes and open file handles.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An inode holds a file's metadata: owner, permissions, size, timestamps, link count, and where its data blocks (extents) are. It does not hold the name. A directory is a file mapping names to inode numbers, so two hard links are two names for one inode. rm is unlink: it removes a name and decrements the link count; space is freed only when the count is 0 and no process still has the file open.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Directory entry (name -> inode#) -> Inode (metadata + extent map) -> data blocks

Hard link: second name, same inode. Symlink: a small file containing a path, can dangle. mv within one file system rewrites directory entries (atomic rename); across file systems it is copy then delete. ext4 and XFS store block locations as extents ("blocks 9000..17191 hold offset 0..32 MB"), and large directories use hashed B-trees so lookup in a million-file directory takes a few reads. ext4 fixes the inode count at mkfs (default roughly one per 16 KB).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ln a b                      # hard link, link count 2
stat a | grep -E 'Inode|Links'
lsof +L1                    # open files with link count 0 (deleted but held)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying rm erases data: it drops a name; blocks are freed later.
  • Thinking the file contains its name.
  • Forgetting that open handles keep deleted files alive.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can hard links not cross file systems? -> Inode numbers are per file system.
  2. Can a process still read a deleted file? -> Yes, through its open fd; /proc/PID/fd/N also works.
  3. Why is rename atomic? -> It is a single directory-entry update inside one journal transaction.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior uses link count plus open count to explain space reclamation and ties it to df -i and lsof +L1 debugging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Deleting a 20 GB log while the process still wrote to it freed nothing until the process was restarted.

questions.promptHtml: When write() returns success, is your data on disk? What does the page cache do on writes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common data-loss misunderstanding in backend code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. write() copies data into page-cache pages marked dirty and returns; the kernel flusher threads write them to disk later, after about 30 s (dirty_expire_centisecs) or when thresholds are hit. A kernel crash or power loss in between loses the data; a process crash does not, since the kernel still holds it. To make it durable you call fsync or fdatasync.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App write() -> page cache (dirty) -> flusher thread later -> disk

Thresholds (defaults, verify on your kernel): vm.dirty_background_ratio 10 starts background flush; vm.dirty_ratio 20 throttles writers and forces synchronous writing. There are two buffers: the libc/stdio buffer (fclose/fflush empties it into the kernel) and the kernel page cache (fsync empties it to the device). Linux uses free RAM as cache: low "free" with healthy "available" in free -m is normal.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback:' /proc/meminfo
free -m

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating write, fflush or close with durability.
  • Reading low "free" as a leak.
  • Dropping caches as a routine "fix".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is read-ahead vs write-back? -> Read-ahead prefetches; write-back delays writes.
  2. Why do writers stall sometimes? -> Dirty memory crosses dirty_ratio.
  3. What does O_DIRECT change? -> Bypasses the cache; alignment rules apply.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior names the two buffers, the dirty thresholds, and which failures lose data (power loss yes, process crash no).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service that logged "saved" after write() lost the last 20 seconds of events on a host power cut.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does journaling solve, how do ext4's ordered, writeback and journal modes differ, and does a journal protect your data?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests crash-consistency thinking and avoids the "journal means safe" myth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Creating a file updates several structures (bitmaps, inode, directory, data); a crash mid-way leaves a corrupt file system, and fsck over a big disk takes hours. A journal is a write-ahead log: log the change, commit it, then apply it, so recovery just replays committed transactions in seconds. ext4's default ordered journals metadata only but writes data blocks first; writeback has no data ordering; journal logs data too and roughly halves write throughput. The journal protects file-system structure, not your last seconds of data; that needs fsync.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Change -> journal blocks -> commit record (with flush/barrier) -> checkpoint to home -> free journal

Crash before commit: transaction discarded as if it never happened. After commit: replayed. Commit interval default commit=5 s, so up to 5 s of updates may be lost though the structure is consistent. writeback can expose old disk contents inside a new file after a crash (security risk). XFS journals metadata only; Btrfs and ZFS use copy-on-write, never overwriting in place, flipping a root pointer atomically. Databases run their own WAL for the same reason.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
dmesg | grep -i ext4         # "recovery complete"
tune2fs -l /dev/sda3 | grep -i journal
mount -o data=ordered /dev/sda3 /data

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying ordered mode journals data.
  • Believing the journal makes writes durable.
  • Choosing data=journal without noticing the double write.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why write data before the metadata commit in ordered mode? -> So no file points to stale garbage blocks.
  2. What is a barrier/flush? -> A command forcing the device cache to media before the commit record counts.
  3. CoW vs journal? -> CoW never overwrites in place and has no replay, at the cost of fragmentation and write amplification.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior separates "structure consistent" from "data durable", and ties it to commit=, fsync and database WALs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a power loss, files existed with zero length because applications had not called fsync, although fsck was clean.

questions.promptHtml: How would you choose between ext4, XFS and a copy-on-write file system for a database or Kafka volume?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A practical choice with real consequences (no XFS shrink, fragmentation on CoW).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both are journaled and extent-based. ext4 is a safe general default, can shrink offline, and is simple. XFS has allocation groups with separate locks, so it scales better with many cores and large files or volumes, but it can only grow. For a database or Kafka I would usually pick XFS or ext4 with noatime. CoW systems (ZFS, Btrfs) give snapshots and checksums but can fragment and amplify writes on write-heavy databases. Block size and inode count are set at mkfs, so choose carefully; changing the file system later means copy out and recreate.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ext4 XFS
Parallelism good allocation groups, very good
Shrink yes (offline) no
Default in Debian/Ubuntu RHEL
Use general, boot big files, DBs, many cores

relatime is the default (atime only if older than mtime or 24 h); noatime removes extra writes. Delayed allocation gives contiguous extents but unflushed files can be zero-length after a crash. ext4 reserves 5% for root (500 GB on a 10 TB disk; tune2fs -m 1). ZFS ARC uses a lot of RAM.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
/dev/nvme2n1 /data/kafka xfs defaults,noatime 0 0
xfs_db -r -c frag /dev/nvme2n1
filefrag -v /data/big.dat

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming XFS can shrink.
  • Choosing CoW for write-heavy DBs without discussing fragmentation.
  • Forgetting mkfs-time decisions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why XFS for many cores? -> Allocation groups mean independent locks and parallel allocation.
  2. What is delayed allocation's risk? -> Data not yet allocated or flushed vanishes in a crash without fsync.
  3. What is tmpfs/overlayfs? -> RAM-backed; layered file system for containers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior bases the choice on workload, shrink/grow needs, operational tooling and the one-way-door nature of mkfs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that picked XFS for a log volume later could not shrink it when moving to a smaller instance and had to rebuild.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does fsync guarantee, and how do you safely replace a config file so a crash never leaves a half-written file?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Data-safety correctness: temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync is a signature senior answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: fsync(fd) forces that file's dirty data and the metadata needed to find it to stable storage before returning. fdatasync skips non-essential metadata like timestamps. For atomic replace: write a temp file in the same directory, fsync it, rename it over the target (atomic on POSIX), then fsync the parent directory so the rename itself is durable. An fsync error must be treated as fatal; retrying can falsely succeed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App fsync() -> FS journal commit -> block layer flush -> disk cache -> media

Costs: consumer SSD 0.5 to 5 ms, datacenter NVMe with power-loss protection 20 to 100 us, HDD 5 to 15 ms. One fsync per commit caps a DB at about 1/latency commits/s (200/s at 5 ms); fix with group commit. The 2018 "fsyncgate": after a failed fsync Linux marked pages clean, so a retry returned success though data was lost; Postgres now panics. Disks can lie about flushes (cheap SSDs without capacitors).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import os
def atomic_write(path, data: bytes):
    tmp = path + ".tmp"
    fd = os.open(tmp, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o644)
    try:
        os.write(fd, data); os.fsync(fd)
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.rename(tmp, path)
    dfd = os.open(os.path.dirname(path) or ".", os.O_RDONLY)
    try: os.fsync(dfd)
    finally: os.close(dfd)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• fclose/flush believed durable.
  • Skipping the directory fsync.
  • Creating the temp file on another file system (rename is then not atomic).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. fsync vs fdatasync? -> fdatasync skips metadata not needed to read data back.
  2. What is group commit? -> Batch many commits into one fsync.
  3. What does O_DSYNC do? -> Each write behaves as followed by fdatasync.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows the full atomic-replace recipe, the cost per device class, group commit and fsyncgate.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A deploy tool wrote config in place; a power cut left an empty file and the host failed to boot until the pattern changed.

questions.contextHtml:
A build server's /var shows errors at 02:10: No space left on device. A teammate sees:

$ df -h /var
/dev/sda3  100G  34G  62G  36% /var
$ touch /var/x
touch: cannot create '/var/x': No space left on device
$ df -i /var
/dev/sda3  6553600 6553600 0 100% /var
$ du -s /var/cache/ci/* | sort -n | tail -2
2.1G  /var/cache/ci/layers
9.8M  /var/cache/ci/tmp      (4.9 million files)

A CI job started creating one tiny file per cache entry last week.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it now and for good?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Delete big files" or "grow the disk"; neither frees inodes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which file system and block size? Who creates the files and are they needed? Can the cache be rebuilt? Is it also near block limits?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete the cache tmp tree (find /var/cache/ci/tmp -type f -delete or rm -rf in batches, mindful of IO); that frees inodes at once.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) inode exhaustion: df -i 100% while blocks are 36%; (b) deleted-but-open files holding blocks (not the case, blocks are free); (c) reserved blocks (no, plenty free); (d) quota (check quota).
  4. How I'd verify each: df -i, df -h, lsof +L1, find /var -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f1-4 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | tail.
  5. Root cause: ext4 allocates a fixed inode table at mkfs (one per 16 KB by default, 6.5M here); 4.9M tiny files plus others exhausted it, so creates fail with ENOSPC even though blocks are free. The error message is misleading.
  6. Fix: Short-term: purge the tiny files. Long-term: stop writing one file per entry (pack into an archive, sqlite or content-addressed bundles); if many small files are legitimate, recreate the volume with more inodes (mkfs.ext4 -N or -T small) or use XFS (dynamic inode allocation).
find /var/cache/ci/tmp -type f -mtime +1 -delete
  1. Prevention: Alert on inode usage (node_filesystem_files_free), retention policy, a lint on the job.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not reformat live; copy-out is downtime. I would not just add disk space.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is rm -rf slow on millions of files? -> Many directory and inode updates; delete incrementally or rsync --delete from an empty dir.
  • Would XFS avoid this? -> Mostly yes; inodes are allocated dynamically within a percentage limit (imaxpct), still bounded.
  • How can you spot it earlier? -> Alert at 80% inode usage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A mail relay stopped accepting messages with 70% free space; every message was a file and inodes ran out.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: deletes big files or grows disk.
  • Hire: checks df -i and purges small files.
  • Strong hire: adds alerting, redesigns storage format, explains inode allocation per file system.

questions.contextHtml:
Disk alert at 98% on /var. An on-call engineer deleted /var/log/app.log (21 GB) at 11:00, but df still shows 98% and the service is writing normally.

$ df -h /var     ->  Use% 98%
$ du -sh /var    ->  12G         (used column says 98G, du says 12G)
$ lsof +L1
COMMAND  PID USER FD TYPE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
java    2310 app   7w REG 21474836480 0  9921 /var/log/app.log (deleted)
questions.promptHtml: Why didn't the space come back, and how do you reclaim it safely without restarting a latency-sensitive service?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "df is stale, wait." Or restarting the production service immediately.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I restart the service at all? Is log rotation (logrotate) configured with copytruncate or a reopen signal? Is the log needed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Truncate through the open fd: : > /proc/2310/fd/7 frees the blocks while the process keeps writing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deleted-but-open file (du 12G vs df 98G gap; lsof shows (deleted)); (b) reserved blocks; (c) snapshots/volume layers; (d) another mount hiding data under the mountpoint.
  4. How I'd verify each: lsof +L1, compare du -x and df, findmnt, check /proc/PID/fd.
  5. Root cause: Space is freed only when link count is 0 and no process has the file open; the JVM still has the file open and keeps writing to the unlinked inode.
  6. Fix: Short-term: truncate via /proc/PID/fd/7. Long-term: use logrotate with a post-rotate reopen (kill -HUP) or copytruncate; better, log to stdout and let the platform rotate; cap log size.
: > /proc/2310/fd/7
  1. Prevention: logrotate config reviewed; alert on disk growth rate and du vs df gap.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: copytruncate can lose a few lines between copy and truncate; a reopen signal needs app support. I would not kill the process just to free space.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can I still read the deleted file? -> Yes, cp /proc/2310/fd/7 /safe/.
  • What if the file was deleted by logrotate itself? -> App ignored the reopen signal; fix the signal handler.
  • Why does du show less? -> du walks directory entries; the unlinked file has none.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team repeatedly "freed" space by deleting logs and wondered why disks kept filling; the gap between df and du was the clue.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits or restarts blindly.
  • Hire: finds deleted-open via lsof and truncates through proc.
  • Strong hire: explains link count + open count, fixes rotation, adds alerting.

questions.contextHtml:
A deploy agent writes /etc/app/config.json on 2,000 hosts. After a rack power event, 37 hosts boot with an empty or truncated config and the app crashes; fsck was clean.

def save_config(path, data):
    with open(path, "w") as f:      # truncates the target first
        f.write(data)
    # file closed here
def save_config_v2(path, data):
    tmp = "/tmp/config.tmp"         # different file system (tmpfs)
    with open(tmp, "w") as f:
        f.write(data)
    os.rename(tmp, path)

v2 was "the fix" and a second power test still lost the file on some hosts (or raised EXDEV).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with both versions, and what is the correct implementation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add f.flush()." That moves data to the kernel, not to disk.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which file systems and mount options? Is partial config ever acceptable? Do other processes read the file during update?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep a last-known-good copy; boot logic falls back to it when validation fails.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) v1 truncates then writes in the cache; a crash leaves empty or partial content; (b) v2 renames across file systems (not atomic; os.rename raises EXDEV); (c) no fsync on data, so the renamed file can be empty after a crash (delayed allocation); (d) no directory fsync, so the rename itself may not persist.
  4. How I'd verify each: findmnt -T /tmp /etc/app; power-fail test or dm-flakey fault injection; strace for fsync.
  5. Root cause: Neither version orders data durability before the name switch. close only flushes the libc buffer; the kernel can persist the rename before the data.
  6. Fix: Temp file in the same directory, fsync file, rename, fsync directory.
def save_config(path, data: bytes):
    d = os.path.dirname(path)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=d)
    try:
        os.write(fd, data); os.fsync(fd)
    finally:
        os.close(fd)
    os.rename(tmp, path)
    dfd = os.open(d, os.O_RDONLY)
    try: os.fsync(dfd)
    finally: os.close(dfd)
  1. Prevention: Shared helper library, power-loss tests in a lab, config checksums validated at boot.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: fsync costs milliseconds; fine for config. I would not use data=journal just to avoid fixing the application.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is rename-over-old-file safe on ext4 without fsync? -> ext4 added heuristics to flush data on rename-replace; do not rely on it across file systems.
  • What if readers hold the file open? -> They keep the old inode and see the new file on reopen.
  • Why must the temp be on the same file system? -> Cross-device rename fails (EXDEV) and is not atomic.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet-wide power maintenance zeroed configs on exactly the hosts that had flushed least recently; the fix was a 12-line helper.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds flush.
  • Hire: temp file, fsync, rename.
  • Strong hire: directory fsync, same-file-system rule, fallback config and power-fail tests.

questions.contextHtml:
An API's p99 jumps from 40 ms to 2 s every few minutes; CPU is 20%. The service writes an audit log and a Postgres database on the same NVMe volume.

$ iostat -x 1
Device   r/s   w/s  rkB/s   wkB/s  await  aqu-sz  %util
nvme0n1  45   2900   360   185000    18.4    53.2   99.8
$ cat /proc/pressure/io
some avg10=62.40 avg60=48.10 avg300=30.00
$ grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback:' /proc/meminfo
Dirty:           3145728 kB
Writeback:        982000 kB
$ perf trace -s -p 4012 -- sleep 5 | grep fsync
fsync    812 calls    total 3910.2 ms    max 640.3 ms

Heap and GC look normal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM" or "tune the JVM". RAM alone enlarges the dirty cache and the later stall.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What process writes 185 MB/s? Is the audit log flushed with fsync? Which file system and journal mode? Did traffic or a backup job change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Throttle or pause the backup or bulk writer (ionice -c3), reduce audit log verbosity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) disk saturation (%util 99.8, aqu-sz 53) from a log flood sharing the device; (b) dirty-page writeback bursts (Dirty 3 GB) throttling writers; (c) journal commit waits behind data (ordered mode makes fsync wait on lots of dirty data); (d) CPU or GC (ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: iostat -x, iotop -o or pidstat -d, /proc/pressure/io, perf trace or strace -T -e fsync, biolatency (bcc).
  5. Root cause: The audit logger floods the shared device; Postgres WAL fsync must wait for the file-system journal commit, which in ordered mode flushes the log's dirty data first. WAL latency becomes commit latency becomes API p99.
  6. Fix: Short-term: put WAL and log on separate devices; lower vm.dirty_background_bytes (for example 256 MB) so writeback starts early and smoothly. Medium: batch and rate-limit audit writes. Long-term: NVMe with power-loss protection, dedicated devices per workload.
sysctl -w vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456
sysctl -w vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824
  1. Prevention: Alerts on %util, await, IO pressure and fsync latency; separate volumes in the design template.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Smaller dirty limits make throughput smoother but reduce bursts absorbed by RAM. I would not add RAM alone or drop caches.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if both must stay on one device? -> cgroup io.max or io.weight for the log writer.
  • Would XFS help? -> Its log is separate from data placement but a shared device is still shared.
  • Could noatime help? -> Minor here; the load is writes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A database fsync histogram showed 600 ms tails exactly when an hourly export ran on the same volume.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes JVM or adds RAM.
  • Hire: identifies shared saturated disk and fsync waits, separates workloads.
  • Strong hire: explains journal ordering, tunes dirty bytes, uses PSI and fsync metrics, adds isolation.

questions.contextHtml:
A batch ETL writes 200 MB/s of output files in 30 s bursts onto a disk that sustains 150 MB/s. The host has 16 GB RAM and defaults dirty_ratio=20, dirty_background_ratio=10. A latency-sensitive neighbour process on the same host sees p99 spikes of 3 to 6 seconds on its small log writes during bursts. top shows kworker/flush busy and the neighbour in D state.

$ grep -E 'Dirty|Writeback' /proc/meminfo
Dirty:   3354624 kB     (about 3.2 GB)
questions.promptHtml: Why do the neighbour's write() calls stall, and how do you fix it at the lowest cost?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Buy a faster disk" or "disable the page cache".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the neighbour in the same cgroup? Do the files need durability? Can ETL be rate limited? Which kernel version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rate-limit the ETL (pv -L, cgroup io.max), or start background writeback sooner.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) dirty memory reaches dirty_ratio (about 3.2 GB of 16 GB) and writers are throttled; (b) disk saturation at 150 MB/s; (c) journal contention; (d) swapping (check vmstat).
  4. How I'd verify each: /proc/meminfo Dirty trend; vmstat 1 (b column, wa); iostat -x; perf trace on the neighbour's write latency.
  5. Root cause: The burst fills the cache faster than the device drains it. Once dirty memory crosses the limit, the kernel throttles every writer to disk speed, including the innocent neighbour whose few KB of log writes now wait in line.
  6. Fix: Short-term: byte-based limits so flushing begins early: vm.dirty_background_bytes=256M, vm.dirty_bytes=1G. Medium: pace ETL output (rate limiter) or call sync_file_range or fdatasync every 64 MB so the backlog stays small; cgroup v2 io controls protect the neighbour. Long-term: faster storage or separate devices.
sysctl -w vm.dirty_background_bytes=268435456 vm.dirty_bytes=1073741824
echo "259:0 wbps=125000000" > /sys/fs/cgroup/etl.slice/io.max
  1. Prevention: Monitor Dirty and writeback, pressure stall info (/proc/pressure/io), test with realistic bursts.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Lower dirty limits reduce write coalescing and add small writes. I would not drop caches or turn on O_SYNC for everyone.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does more RAM make it worse? -> The cache absorbs bigger bursts, then stalls longer when the limit is hit.
  • Does O_DIRECT help? -> It bypasses the cache but exposes disk speed directly.
  • cgroup v1 vs v2 writeback? -> v2 supports per-cgroup writeback throttling; v1 does not (verify on your kernel).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An hourly export made unrelated services stall; lowering the dirty limits fixed hours of "mystery latency".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: buys hardware or blames the app.
  • Hire: explains dirty thresholds and tunes them.
  • Strong hire: computes absorption, uses cgroup io limits and pacing, discusses trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
A payments ledger service commits each transaction with an fsync on its WAL. Measured with strace:

fdatasync(12) = 0 <0.004912>
fdatasync(12) = 0 <0.005104>

Throughput tops out at 200 commits/s per instance on a cheap cloud SSD; the business needs 5,000 commits/s per instance and must not lose acknowledged payments. The team proposes synchronous_commit=off (Postgres) or appendfsync no (Redis).
questions.promptHtml: What is the ceiling and how do you hit 5,000/s without breaking durability? Which options would you refuse?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn off fsync." That loses acknowledged payments.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is acked-means-durable mandatory? Are synchronous replicas available? What device, and does it have power-loss protection? What latency SLA per commit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for correctness; I do not weaken durability under pressure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) one fsync per commit gives 1/5 ms = 200/s; (b) device flush latency is the bottleneck; (c) CPU is irrelevant; (d) network is a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_test_fsync, fio --fsync=1, strace timings, WAL stats.
  5. Root cause: Serial fsync latency sets the commit rate. 5,000/s needs batching or a faster flush.
  6. Fix: (1) Group commit: concurrent transactions share one fsync (commit_delay and commit_siblings in Postgres, binlog group commit in MySQL). With 25 commits per 5 ms flush that gives 5,000/s while each commit still waits for durability. (2) Enterprise NVMe with power-loss protection (flush in 20 to 100 us, 10,000+/s). (3) Synchronous replication to 2 nodes in different failure domains if the SLA tolerates a network round trip in place of a local fsync. (4) A separate WAL device. I refuse synchronous_commit=off and appendfsync no for payments: the loss window (about 600 ms of acked commits) is a business decision, not an optimisation.
sync commit + group commit : durable, higher throughput, a few ms more latency
synchronous_commit=off     : consistent, but may lose the last ~600 ms of acked commits
  1. Prevention: Track fsync latency histograms; test on production-class disks; document the durability contract.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Group commit adds up to a few ms of latency; hardware costs money; replication adds RTT. I would not trust a drive without proof it honours flushes (power-loss tests).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which workloads can use async commit? -> Metrics, caches, non-financial events.
  • What about Kafka? -> It does not fsync each message; durability comes from replication with acks=all.
  • How do disks "lie"? -> A volatile cache acknowledges the flush early; enterprise SSDs have capacitors.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A move from local NVMe to network volumes cut commit rates 10x until group commit and a separate WAL volume were configured.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables fsync.
  • Hire: group commit and faster device.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the ceiling, weighs sync replication, separates loss windows by workload, tests flush honesty.

questions.subtopic: Changing file system under live traffic
questions.contextHtml:
A 12-broker Kafka cluster (each broker an 8 TB ext4 volume, 5% reserved, about 86% full) shows long segment deletes and allocation contention. Leadership wants XFS and better disk use, with no downtime and a 3-replica setup (min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all). Retention is 3 days; cluster traffic is 400 MB/s in.

$ tune2fs -l /dev/nvme1n1 | grep -E 'Reserved block count|Block count'
Reserved block count: 107374182    (5%)
$ mount | grep kafka
/dev/nvme1n1 on /data/kafka type ext4 (rw,relatime)
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration and say what you change in mount options and tuning.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Convert in place" (no such tool) or "stop the cluster at night".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can brokers be taken out one at a time with replication intact? Is there spare capacity to absorb re-replication? Are replicas rack-aware? What benchmark shows XFS helps?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Free space first: tune2fs -m 1 (reserved 5% down to 1%) frees about 320 GB per broker with no downtime; mount noatime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) deleting large segment files stalls on ext4; (b) fragmentation or allocation contention; (c) the disk is near full (86%) which hurts allocation; (d) kernel version effects.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare broker I/O wait and segment delete times, filefrag, benchmark ext4 vs XFS with the real workload on one canary broker.
  5. Root cause: The workload (large append-only segments, bulk deletes, many cores) matches XFS strengths, but the benefit must be measured, not assumed.
  6. Fix (plan): There is no in-place conversion: it is copy-out and re-create. Rolling, one broker at a time: confirm all partitions are in sync, controlled shutdown (leadership moves), unmount, mkfs.xfs, mount defaults,noatime, start the broker so it re-replicates from peers (about 7 TB). Throttle replication (leader.replication.throttled.rate) so production traffic is safe; wait until under-replicated partitions are 0 before the next broker. Never take two brokers of the same replica set out together with min.insync.replicas=2.
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/nvme1n1
echo '/dev/nvme1n1 /data/kafka xfs defaults,noatime 0 0' >> /etc/fstab
  1. Prevention: Canary with metrics, capacity planning, disk usage alerts at 75%.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Re-replication adds network and disk load and reduces the redundancy margin for days; XFS cannot shrink later. I would not do two brokers at once or skip the canary.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 matter? -> One broker down still allows writes; two would stop them.
  • Could we use fewer, larger brokers? -> Maybe, but capacity and failure domains decide.
  • What if the canary shows no gain? -> Keep ext4 and only do the tune2fs -m and noatime changes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A reserved-block tweak freed more headroom than the whole file-system migration would have, and avoided a month of risk.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries in-place conversion or downtime.
  • Hire: rolling per-broker rebuild with replication throttle.
  • Strong hire: starts with measurement and the free tune2fs -m win, respects ISR constraints and rollback.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review: a datacenter lost power for 8 seconds. On 14 ext4 hosts running a metadata service, the file system recovered cleanly (recovery complete, fsck clean), yet 3 hosts had zero-length index files created in the final seconds, and the application restarted with missing data. The service writes with plain write() and close(), journal mode is the default, commit=5.

$ dmesg | grep -i ext4
EXT4-fs (sda3): recovery complete
EXT4-fs (sda3): mounted filesystem with ordered data mode.
$ ls -l /data/index/seg-9912.idx
-rw-r--r-- 1 app app 0 ... seg-9912.idx
questions.promptHtml: What happened, whose fault is it, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ext4 has a bug" or "switch to data=journal."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the app call fsync anywhere? Do the drives have power-loss protection? Are write caches on? What is the durability promise to users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rebuild missing segments from replicas or backup; mark affected hosts for repair.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the application never fsynced; the name and size 0 were committed while the data was still dirty in RAM (delayed allocation); (b) the drive's volatile cache lied; (c) an ext4 bug (unlikely); (d) fsck problem (no, clean).
  4. How I'd verify each: Check code or strace for fsync; check hdparm -W and the drive spec for power-loss protection; replay on a test rig with power cuts.
  5. Root cause: The journal guarantees file-system structure, not application data. In ordered mode data is written before the metadata commit only for blocks already allocated; with delayed allocation the data was not yet allocated. With a 5 s commit interval, everything in the last seconds is at risk without fsync. The file system behaved as designed.
  6. Fix: Short-term: follow temp file, fsync, rename, fsync directory; fsync critical files at the commit point. Medium: replicate index data so losing one host is repairable; checksum files on load and rebuild on mismatch. Long-term: drives with power-loss protection; batch fsyncs to limit cost.
with open(tmp, "wb") as f:
    f.write(data); f.flush(); os.fsync(f.fileno())
os.rename(tmp, final)
  1. Prevention: Power-loss test in the lab (fault injection) before release; durability documented per data class; fsync latency metrics.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: data=journal doubles writes and still does not give application-level atomicity; commit=1 shrinks the window but is not a guarantee. I would not blame the file system.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the file exist with size 0? -> The name and inode were committed, the data was not allocated or written yet.
  • Would XFS differ? -> Same class of behaviour; it also needs fsync.
  • Is Postgres vulnerable? -> No, it fsyncs WAL on commit; that is its contract.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team's "journaled file system" assumption failed at the first real power event; the fix was a small fsync-aware storage layer for critical writes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the file system or chooses data=journal.
  • Hire: identifies missing fsync and fixes the write pattern.
  • Strong hire: explains delayed allocation vs ordered mode, replication and checksum design, fault-injection testing.
